newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala central bank weighs helping quetzal.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala central bank weighs helping quetzal.

text.p: Guatemala's central bank is considering a plan to intervene in order to stabilize its weakening currency, the quetzal, Central Bank President Edin Velasquez said on Thursday.
"We are observing the market. If it stabilizes then we won't have to intervene," Velasquez, who took over his post in June, told Reuters in an interview.
The government has not intervened in the currency market since October when it issued quetzal-denominated certificates of deposit -- the same plan being considered now.
"The idea is to remove quetzals (from the market) to reduce pressure on the exchange rate. We don't want to do it again, because the idea is not to use that method any more," Velasquez said.
"But the abnormal movement (in the exchange rate) worries us because there are too many quetzals," he added.
The quetzal has weakened since July 6 when it reached a 20-month high of 5.89 to the dollar. On Thursday the average bank rate for buying dollars was 6.08.
July and August are traditionally months of high demand for dollars to buy year-end imports, Velasquez said.

Guatemala received an influx of $150 million after issuing its debut Eurobond July 28, but that did not affect the quetzal because the authorities kept the proceeds off the market, setting it aside for government projects, Velazquez said.
He said Guatemala's gross domestic product would grow as forecast at approximately 4.1 percent in 1997, up from 3.1 percent in 1996 -- its lowest level since 1990.
"Investment in petroleum exploration in what used to be war-torn areas and some government infrastructure programs will contribute to 4.1 percent growth this year," he said.
But high prices for coffee, Guatemala's number one export, will be the main contributor to healthy growth this year, he added.
Guatemala's 36-year civil war came to an official end in December 1996 when the government and leftist rebels signed a peace accord. Since then GDP has grown and inflation declined.
Year-on-year inflation was 7.98 percent on July 31 compared to 11.60 at the end of July 1996. Accumulated inflation was 4.08 percent by the end of July, compared to 6.85 percent a year ago.
"We've seen a significant slow down in inflation," Velasquez said.
